facts.fact_text: Immediately after the announcement of the preliminary results of the 19 February 2008 Armenian presidential election, Mr Ter-Petrosyan called on his supporters to gather at Freedom Square (also known as Opera Square) in central Yerevan to protest against alleged irregularities in the election process.
From 20 February 2008 onwards, nationwide daily protest rallies were held by Mr Ter-Petrosyan's supporters, with their main meeting place being Freedom Square and the surrounding park in Yerevan.
The rallies at Freedom Square, held during the daytime and late into the night, attracted at times tens of thousands of people.
The applicant was an active participant in the rallies at Freedom Square and was often on the podium.
The applicant made a speech on the first day of the rallies at Freedom Square.

The applicant alleged that suddenly, without any prior warning or orders to disperse, the police forces, shouting loudly, attacked the demonstrators at Freedom Square, most of whom were still asleep in their tents, violently beating them with rubber batons and destroying the camp.
The applicant alleged that Mr Ter-Petrosyan was immediately arrested and taken away from Freedom Square on 1 March 2008.
The applicant alleged that he and other activists were then pursued by the police through the streets and arrested.
The events of 1 March 2008 in Yerevan resulted in ten deaths, including eight civilians.
Following the events of 1 March 2008, a state of emergency was declared by the incumbent President Kocharyan.
The state of emergency declared by President Kocharyan prohibited, inter alia, the holding of any further rallies and other mass public events for a period of twenty days.
Many participants in the post-election rallies, including a number of opposition leaders, were charged and stood trial within the scope of criminal cases nos. 62202508 and 62202608.

According to a handwritten document entitled "the record of bringing-in", the applicant was "brought in" to Kentron Police Station on 1 March 2008 at around 6.30 a.m. by three police officers, E.R., H.S. and A.A., from 1 Grigor Lusavorich Street.

The record of bringing-in stated that the applicant was brought to Kentron Police Station "for organising unauthorised demonstrations at Freedom Square in support of Mr Ter-Petrosyan, resisting police officers and disobeying their lawful orders".
On 23 October 2008 the Yerevan Criminal Court found the applicant guilty under Article 235 § 4 and Article 316 §§ 1 and 2 of the Armenian Criminal Code.
The Yerevan Criminal Court sentenced the applicant under Article 316 § 2 of the Armenian Criminal Code to five years' imprisonment.

The decision instituting criminal case no. 62202508 stated that after the announcement of the preliminary results of the 19 February 2008 presidential election, Mr Levon Ter-Petrosyan, members of parliament K.S. and S.M., the chief editor of Haykakan Zhamanak daily newspaper N.P., and others organised and held mass public events at Yerevan's Freedom Square in violation of the procedure prescribed by law and incited disobedience to the decisions ordering an end to the events held in violation of the procedure prescribed by law.

The decision instituting criminal case no. 62202508 stated that on 1 March 2008 at around 6 a.m., when the police took measures aimed at forcibly ending the public events held in violation of the procedure prescribed by law in compliance with the requirements of section 14 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, the organisers and participants of the events, disobeying the lawful orders of the police officers who were performing their official duties, committed a life- and health-threatening assault on them with clubs, metal rods and other adapted objects, causing the police officers injuries of varied severity.

Section 14 of the Armenian Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act (2004-2011) provides that the police are entitled to decide to terminate a public event and to order the organisers to terminate the event, by allowing them a reasonable time-limit to do so, if, inter alia, the mass public event is being held without notification, except for the cases in which a non-mass public event spontaneously turns into a mass public event.

Section 14 of the Armenian Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act (2004-2011) provides that the police are entitled to terminate forcibly a public event only if (a) the order to terminate an event is not immediately announced to the participants by the organiser; or (b) the order to terminate the public event has not been complied with within the fixed time-limit and its continuation poses a real threat to the life and health of others, State and public security, public order or public or private property.

The Government claimed that the reason for the police operation of 1 March 2008 at Freedom Square was information obtained on 29 February 2008 by the Armenian Police and National Security Service, according to which a large number of weapons, including metal rods, wooden clubs, firearms, grenades and explosives, were to be distributed to the protesters to incite provocative actions and mass disorder in Yerevan on 1 March 2008.
The Government claimed that the police operation of 1 March 2008 aimed to verify the intelligence information about weapons being distributed to protesters.

The decision instituting criminal case no. 62202508 stated that after the announcement of the preliminary results of the 19 February 2008 presidential election, Mr Levon Ter-Petrosyan, members of parliament K.S. and S.M., the chief editor of Haykakan Zhamanak daily newspaper N.P., and others organised and held mass public events at Yerevan's Freedom Square in violation of the procedure prescribed by law and incited disobedience to the decisions ordering an end to the events held in violation of the procedure prescribed by law.

The decision instituting criminal case no. 62202508 stated that on 1 March 2008 at around 6 a.m., when the police took measures aimed at forcibly ending the public events held in violation of the procedure prescribed by law in compliance with the requirements of section 14 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, the organisers and participants of the events, disobeying the lawful orders of the police officers who were performing their official duties, committed a life- and health-threatening assault on them with clubs, metal rods and other adapted objects, causing the police officers injuries of varied severity.
The applicant alleged that on 1 March 2008 at around 6 a.m. the police arrived at Freedom Square.

The applicant alleged that the several hundred demonstrators camping at Freedom Square on 1 March 2008 were mostly still asleep when the police arrived, although some were awake, having been informed in advance about the arrival of a large number of police officers.

The applicant alleged that Mr Ter-Petrosyan was also at Freedom Square on 1 March 2008 and addressed the demonstrators, saying: "We see that police forces have arrived at the square. Please, do not have any contact with them and do not touch them in any way. Please keep your distance from them. Let us wait and see what they want from us. If they have something to tell us, we are ready to listen. Please, be patient and peaceful".
The applicant alleged that after Mr Ter-Petrosyan's address there was silence for about a minute, by which time the police forces had already encircled Freedom Square with a triple cordon.

The applicant alleged that suddenly, without any prior warning or orders to disperse, the police forces, shouting loudly, attacked the demonstrators at Freedom Square, most of whom were still asleep in their tents, violently beating them with rubber batons and destroying the camp.
The Government contested the applicant's allegations regarding the police operation of 1 March 2008 at Freedom Square.

The Government claimed that members of the relevant police force, without being equipped with any protective gear, arrived at Freedom Square where about 800 to 900 demonstrators armed with metal rods and wooden clubs had gathered waiting for the police.

The Government claimed that the demonstrators attacked the police officers on 1 March 2008, hitting them and throwing stones, pointed metal objects and Molotov cocktails at them, as a result of which numerous police officers were injured.

By a letter of 27 March 2008 the Deputy Chief of the Armenian Police replied to the Chief of the Special Investigative Service's request of 10 March 2008, stating that the organisers and participants in the unauthorised rallies held between 20 and 29 February 2008 had, on numerous occasions, been informed about the unlawful nature of those events.

The Deputy Chief of the Armenian Police's letter of 27 March 2008 stated that the police operation of 1 March 2008 was based on intelligence information received the previous day by the police and the national security service, according to which a large quantity of metal rods, wooden clubs, firearms, grenades and explosives was to be distributed to the demonstrators in order to instigate mass disorder.
The Deputy Chief of the Armenian Police's letter of 27 March 2008 stated that the aim of the 1 March 2008 operation was to verify the intelligence information and to inspect the area.

The Deputy Chief of the Armenian Police's letter of 27 March 2008 stated that a number of unarmed police officers had entered Opera Square (Freedom Square) where they were attacked by 800-900 demonstrators armed with metal rods and wooden clubs, who were expecting the arrival of the police.
The Deputy Chief of the Armenian Police's letter of 27 March 2008 stated that the police officers were beaten and stones, pointed metal objects and Molotov cocktails were thrown at them.

The Deputy Chief of the Armenian Police's letter of 27 March 2008 stated that in order to prevent the disorder, an on-the-spot decision had been taken to engage the auxiliary police forces, which had been deployed earlier on the approaches to Freedom Square and had been equipped with helmets, shields and rubber batons.
The Deputy Chief of the Armenian Police's letter of 27 March 2008 stated that the engagement of the auxiliary police forces resulted in the demonstrators fleeing Freedom Square.

The Deputy Chief of the Armenian Police's letter of 27 March 2008 stated that the operation was carried out between 7 and 7.30 a.m. and was followed by a search, as a result of which numerous specially adapted metal objects, arms, ammunition and Molotov cocktails were found.

The Armenian Ombudsman's Report stated that the 1 March 2008 events started with the forcible termination of the peaceful sit-in at Freedom Square, when at 6.40 a.m. police officers wearing anti-riot gear and carrying shields and batons attacked the demonstrators who were at Freedom Square.

The Armenian Ombudsman's Report stated that from a formal point of view, the demonstration that lasted from 21 February to 1 March 2008 did not comply with the requirements of law because the Mayor of Yerevan had neither been notified nor taken note of a demonstration to be held.

The Armenian Ombudsman's Report quoted the OSCE/ODIHR report as stating: "From 21 February to early morning on 1 March protesters held a peaceful, though not formally authorised, assembly (and tent camp) in Freedom Square in Yerevan and conducted numerous peaceful processions. Speakers at the assembly announced that their aim was to annul and repeat the election. Until 1 March, the authorities overall tolerated the protests."

The Armenian Ombudsman's Report quoted President Robert Kocharyan as stating: "The unauthorised demonstrations were not terminated by the police for nine consecutive days only for one reason: I prohibited them to do so. The reason was the post-election recount and the appeal process. I believed that a dispersal of demonstrations would be perceived as an attempt by the authorities to undermine the recount or the appeal process."
The Armenian Ombudsman's Report stated that on 29 February 2008 President Robert Kocharyan stated that among available solutions was the "cleaning of the Square" by the police.

The Armenian Ombudsman's Report stated that while it is true that every day prior to 1 March the police announced over loudspeakers that the demonstration was unlawful and ordered the demonstrators to end it, no such order was made in the morning of 1 March 2008 and no time-limit was given to the demonstrators to end the demonstration as required by section 14 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act.

The Armenian Ombudsman's Report stated that there were two police cordons at Freedom Square on 1 March 2008: one right on the square and the other one along the four adjacent streets, and that the purpose of those cordons was to keep everyone out so that the demonstration ended.

The Armenian Ombudsman's Report stated that not all the persons gathered at Freedom Square were purported criminals, and that the police operation directly resulted in the forcible termination of the demonstration, with demonstrators being chased far beyond Freedom Square.
The Armenian Ombudsman's Report stated that to date, not a single criminal case had been initiated against any police officer, even for excessive use of physical force and of special means.

The European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment's report stated that practically all the persons who had been detained by law enforcement officers on 1 March 2008 alleged that they had been physically ill-treated at the time of their apprehension, even though they apparently had not offered resistance, with the ill-treatment consisting mainly of truncheon blows, kicks and punches to the body and head, and being pushed to the ground and dragged into a police vehicle.

The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights' report of 20 March 2008 stated that it seemed clear that excessive use of force was used by police and the security forces, as confirmed by the sheer number of injured persons and passing civilians registered in the hospitals as well as found in places of detention, having beating marks, concussion and open scars on their skulls.

The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights' report of 20 March 2008 stated that on 13 March 2008 the Prosecutor General informed that over 95 persons had been arrested for having organized or participated in demonstrations and mass disturbances of public order, and that most of the arrested had been charged with disturbing public order, illegal possession of arms, incitement to violent acts, and resisting violently police arrest.

The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights' report of 20 March 2008 stated that detainees claimed that the police had used excessive force in connection with arrest, and that it seemed that beating took place in a number of cases at the time of arrest and during transportation of the apprehended to the different precincts.

The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights' report of 20 March 2008 stated that there had been delays in the registration of arrests, that access to defence lawyers had in some instances been delayed, that family members or relatives had not been informed of the detainee's whereabouts, and that persons apprehended had not been promptly informed of the charges against them.

The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights' report of 20 March 2008 stated that the judges seemed not to have entered into a serious test of the charges, the legality of the apprehension and the proportionality of deprivation of liberty, and that the courts seemed to have routinely granted pre-trial detention of two months to allow the prosecutor to investigate further and prepare the charges and the criminal case.

The European Parliament's Resolution of 13 March 2008 stated that opposition supporters began peaceful rallies on 20 February 2008 in Yerevan to protest against the election result and demand a rerun, and that on the evening of 1 March 2008, after eleven days of protest by opposition supporters, violence erupted when police moved into Freedom Square in central Yerevan to disperse the protesters camped out in tents, leaving eight people dead, including one police officer, and dozens injured.

The European Parliament's Resolution of 13 March 2008 expressed concern at the violent police crackdown on opposition demonstrations, leading to the death of eight citizens including one police officer, with over a hundred injured, and called for a prompt, thorough, transparent, independent and impartial investigation of the events of 1 March 2008, including an independent investigation of the police intervention during the dispersal of the demonstration.

Human Rights Watch's report stated that statements taken from demonstrators and bystanders suggested that the first police action in the early morning of 1 March 2008 against the Freedom Square tent encampment entailed excessive use of force, without warning and in the absence, at the start, of resistance.

Human Rights Watch's report stated that several witnesses interviewed separately by Human Rights Watch consistently described that some time shortly after 6 a.m. on 1 March 2008, while it was still dark, hundreds of Special Forces police in riot armour, with helmets, plastic shields, and rubber truncheons, started approaching Freedom Square from Tumanyan Street and Mashtots Avenue, surrounded the square and stood there for a few minutes.

Human Rights Watch's report stated that according to Mr Ter-Petrosyan's account, he addressed the protesters asking them to step back from the police line and then to stay where they were and wait for instructions from the police, and also warned the police that there were women and children among the demonstrators.

Human Rights Watch's report stated that according to multiple witnesses, even before Mr Ter-Petrosyan finished his address, police advanced towards the demonstrators in several lines, beating their truncheons against their plastic shields, making no audible demand for anyone to disperse nor giving any indication of the purpose of their presence, and then without any warning, riot police attacked the demonstrators, using rubber truncheons, iron sticks, and electric shock batons.
Human Rights Watch's report stated that as a result of the early morning police actions on Freedom Square on 1 March 2008, 31 people were officially reported to be injured, including six policemen.

Human Rights Watch's report stated that the police claimed that after the demonstrators were dispersed they found a stock of real and makeshift weapons, including three guns, 15 grenades, two bullet cases and 138 bullets of various calibres, plastic explosives, a big number of makeshift weapons, syringes and drugs, but that all witnesses and victims interviewed by Human Rights Watch claimed that the alleged arms cache was planted after the demonstration was dispersed.

Human Rights Watch's report stated that the chairman of the ad hoc parliamentary commission established to investigate the 1 March 2008 events told Human Rights Watch in January 2009 that he had not seen any evidence linking the arms cache to the demonstration's participants or organizers.
The events of 1 March 2008 in Yerevan resulted in ten deaths, including eight civilians.
The events of 1 March 2008 in Yerevan resulted in numerous injured persons.
On 3 June 2008 the applicant applied to the General Prosecutor requesting that criminal proceedings be instituted and an investigation be carried out into the fact of his ill-treatment.

In his application to the General Prosecutor of 3 June 2008, the applicant submitted that the circumstances of his arrest involved an offence against him since he had been beaten and tortured, but no assessment had been given to that circumstance in the context of the criminal case against him.
No decision was taken on the applicant's application of 3 June 2008 to the General Prosecutor requesting an investigation into his ill-treatment.
The Armenian Ombudsman's Report stated that to date, not a single criminal case had been initiated against any police officer, even for excessive use of physical force and of special means.

The European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment's report stated that practically all the persons who had been detained by law enforcement officers on 1 March 2008 alleged that they had been physically ill-treated at the time of their apprehension, even though they apparently had not offered resistance, with the ill-treatment consisting mainly of truncheon blows, kicks and punches to the body and head, and being pushed to the ground and dragged into a police vehicle.

The European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment's report stated that in some cases the beating had apparently continued during transportation to police establishments and upon arrival there, and that according to several of the persons alleging ill-treatment, some of the law enforcement officials involved were wearing masks and did not have any form of identification on their clothing.

The European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment's report stated that the delegation received a few allegations of physical ill-treatment at the time of questioning by the police, consisting essentially of slaps, punches, kicks and truncheon blows, apparently inflicted with the purpose of obtaining confessions or information implicating other persons.

The European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment's report stated that certain of the persons who made allegations of ill-treatment were found on examination by a medical member of the delegation to display physical marks or conditions consistent with their allegations, and that the medical documentation at the penitentiary establishments visited also contained descriptions of various injuries observed by prison doctors during the initial examination of a number of persons admitted in the two weeks preceding the delegation's visit.

The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights' report of 20 March 2008 stated that it seemed clear that excessive use of force was used by police and the security forces, as confirmed by the sheer number of injured persons and passing civilians registered in the hospitals as well as found in places of detention, having beating marks, concussion and open scars on their skulls.

The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights' report of 20 March 2008 stated that detainees claimed that the police had used excessive force in connection with arrest, and that it seemed that beating took place in a number of cases at the time of arrest and during transportation of the apprehended to the different precincts.

The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights' Summary of Findings of 29 September 2008 stated that to date, no law enforcement officials had been charged in connection with the 1 March 2008 events.

The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe/Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights' Final Report stated that of the 19 cases featuring police witnesses, 13 defendants were charged with resistance to the police under Article 316 of the Armenian Criminal Code, and that at least six defendants made allegations of police misconduct or brutality against them at the time of apprehension, which were not investigated and no tainted evidence was excluded by the judges.
